lead: A shaft carries power from a motor to a machine. Its pulleys and gears bend it, the power twists it, and a helical gear or worm also pushes it along its axis. Static design finds the combined stress at the outer surface, compares it with an allowable stress from a failure theory, and picks a standard diameter.

sections.h3: Shafts, axles and the loads they carry

blocks.text: A shaft rotates and transmits torque. An axle carries rotating parts, such as the wheels of a railway wagon, but transmits no torque, so it is designed for bending only. A spindle is a short shaft, as in a lathe headstock.

The torque comes from the power: T = 60P/(2πN), with P in W, N in rpm and T in N·m. The bending moment comes from the forces on the shaft. A belt pulley of diameter D with tight-side tension T<sub>1</sub> and slack-side tension T<sub>2</sub> pulls the shaft with T<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>2</sub> and passes the torque (T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>)D/2. A spur gear gives a tangential force F<sub>t</sub> = 2T/D and a radial force F<sub>r</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan 20°; both bend the shaft, and F<sub>t</sub> also gives the torque.

items: Treat the shaft as a beam on its bearings; find the reactions and draw the bending moment diagram.
If forces act in two planes, draw a diagram for each and combine them: M = √(M<sub>V</sub>² + M<sub>H</sub>²).
The section with the largest M and T fixes the diameter.

sections.h3: Equivalent torque, equivalent moment and the ASME code

blocks.text: At the surface of a solid shaft of diameter d, bending gives σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd³) along the axis and torque gives τ = 16T/(πd³). With σ<sub>y</sub> = 0, the principal stresses are σ<sub>1,2</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub>/2 ± √((σ<sub>b</sub>/2)² + τ²).
Maximum shear stress theory (Guest), used for ductile steel: τmax = √((σb/2)² + τ²) = 16√(M² + T²)/(πd³). The bracket is the equivalent torque:

Te = √(M² + T²); τallow = 16Te/(πd³)
Te is the torque that alone gives the same maximum shear stress as M and T together.

Maximum normal stress theory (Rankine), used for brittle material: σ1 = 16[M + √(M² + T²)]/(πd³). The equivalent bending moment is Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)], and σallow = 32Me/(πd³). Where both are asked, take the larger d.

The ASME code adds shock factors and an allowable stress. Use Kb M and Kt T in place of M and T: for a rotating shaft, Kb = 1.5 and Kt = 1.0 for gradual load, up to Kb = 3.0 and Kt = 3.0 for heavy shock. The allowable shear stress is the smaller of 0.30Syt and 0.18Sut, where Syt and Sut are the yield and ultimate tensile strengths, and it is cut by 25 % when the shaft has a keyway.

An axial force P adds a direct stress σ<sub>a</sub> = 4P/(πd²). It changes σ<sub>x</sub>, so T<sub>e</sub> no longer covers the case. Use σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub> and τ<sub>max</sub> = ½√(σ<sub>x</sub>² + 4τ²). Bending makes one side of the shaft tensile and the other compressive, so the worst point is the side where the bending stress has the same sign as the axial stress: there |σ<sub>x</sub>| = σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub>.

A hollow shaft of outer diameter do and inner diameter di, with k = di/do, has τ = 16T/(πdo³(1 − k⁴)) and σb = 32M/(πdo³(1 − k⁴)), so Te and Me work as before with d³ replaced by do³(1 − k⁴). The axial area is πdo²(1 − k²)/4. The bored-out core carries little stress, so a hollow shaft is lighter for the same strength, which is why propeller shafts are hollow.

examples.question: A shaft runs on two bearings A and B, 900 mm apart. A pulley of 400 mm diameter sits 300 mm from A and receives 10 kW at 500 rpm from a vertical belt with tension ratio T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> = 3. The shaft is of steel with S<sub>yt</sub> = 380 MPa and S<sub>ut</sub> = 640 MPa and has a keyway. The load is gradually applied (K<sub>b</sub> = 1.5, K<sub>t</sub> = 1.0). Find the shaft diameter by the ASME code. Neglect the pulley weight.
steps: Belt tensions: (T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) × 0.2 m = 190.99, so T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub> = 954.93 N. With T<sub>1</sub> = 3T<sub>2</sub>: T<sub>2</sub> = 477.46 N, T<sub>1</sub> = 1432.39 N. Downward pull on the shaft W = T<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>2</sub> = 1909.86 N.
Largest bending moment, under the pulley: M = R<sub>A</sub> × 0.3 = 381.97 N·m.
Allowable shear stress: 0.30 × 380 = 114 MPa and 0.18 × 640 = 115.2 MPa; take 114 MPa. With the keyway, τ = 0.75 × 114 = 85.5 MPa.
Equivalent torque: T<sub>e</sub> = √((K<sub>b</sub> M)² + (K<sub>t</sub> T)²) = √(572.96² + 190.99²) = 603.95 N·m = 603 950 N·mm.
Diameter: d³ = 16T<sub>e</sub>/(πτ) = 16 × 603 950/(π × 85.5) = 35 973 mm³, so d = 33.0 mm.
examples.answer: d = 33.0 mm; adopt the next standard size, 35 mm. At 35 mm, τ = 71.7 MPa ≤ 85.5 MPa.

examples.question: A hollow shaft (d<sub>i</sub>/d<sub>o</sub> = 0.5) transmits 15 kW at 900 rpm with K<sub>t</sub> = 1.5, and carries a steady bending moment of 300 N·m and an axial compression of 10 kN. τ<sub>allow</sub> = 40 MPa. Find d<sub>o</sub> and compare its mass with the 38 mm solid shaft that suits the same duty.
steps: With k = 0.5 and d<sub>o</sub> in m: A = 0.5890d<sub>o</sub>², Z = (π/32)d<sub>o</sub>³(1 − k⁴) = 0.09204d<sub>o</sub>³, Z<sub>p</sub> = 2Z. So σ<sub>b</sub> = 3259.5/d<sub>o</sub>³, σ<sub>a</sub> = 16 977/d<sub>o</sub>² and τ = 1296.9/d<sub>o</sub>³ (Pa).
On the compression side, |σ<sub>x</sub>| = σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub>. Setting ½√(σ<sub>x</sub>² + 4τ²) = 40 MPa and solving by trial gives d<sub>o</sub> = 38.9 mm.
Check with d<sub>o</sub> = 39 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 54.95 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 11.16 MPa, σ<sub>x</sub> = 66.11 MPa, τ = 21.86 MPa, τ<sub>max</sub> = ½√(66.11² + 4 × 21.86²) = 39.6 MPa ≤ 40 MPa.
Mass ratio for equal length: hollow area/solid area = 39² × 0.75/38² = 0.79.
examples.answer: d<sub>o</sub> = 39 mm and d<sub>i</sub> = 19.5 mm. The hollow shaft is about 21 % lighter than the 38 mm solid shaft.

traps: Using T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) when an axial load acts. The axial stress changes σ<sub>x</sub>, so work with σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub> and τ<sub>max</sub> = ½√(σ<sub>x</sub>² + 4τ²).
Checking the side where bending tension and axial compression partly cancel. The design point is where they add.
Taking the belt pull as T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>. The shaft is bent by T<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>2</sub>; only the torque uses the difference.
Mixing units: with τ in MPa, T<sub>e</sub> must be in N·mm.

quiz.q: Write the equivalent torque and the equivalent bending moment for a solid shaft under M and T.
quiz.a: T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) (maximum shear stress theory); M<sub>e</sub> = ½[M + √(M² + T²)] (maximum normal stress theory).

quiz.q: Why can T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) not be used when an axial load P acts?
quiz.a: P adds σ<sub>a</sub> = 4P/(πd²), so on the worst side σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub> and τ<sub>max</sub> = ½√(σ<sub>x</sub>² + 4τ²); T<sub>e</sub> leaves σ<sub>a</sub> out.

quiz.q: What do the ASME shock factors K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> do, and which values suit a gradually loaded rotating shaft?
quiz.a: They raise M and T for shock and fatigue in service: K<sub>b</sub> = 1.5 and K<sub>t</sub> = 1.0 for gradual load.

quiz.q: A solid shaft of 40 mm diameter carries M = 500 N·m and T = 400 N·m with no axial load. Find the maximum shear stress.
A hollow shaft of 50 mm outer and 30 mm inner diameter transmits 200 N·m only. Find the shear stress.
At one point a shaft has bending stress 60 MPa (tension), axial compression 20 MPa and shear 30 MPa. Find τ<sub>max</sub> there; is this the design point?
quiz.a: Here σ<sub>x</sub> = 60 − 20 = 40 MPa and τ<sub>max</sub> = √(20² + 30²) = 36.1 MPa. It is not the design point: on the opposite side σ<sub>x</sub> = −(60 + 20) = −80 MPa and τ<sub>max</sub> = √(40² + 30²) = 50 MPa, which governs.

beyond: Real shafts fail mostly by fatigue, so industry adds an endurance check at every shoulder and keyway (Soderberg, Goodman or the ASME elliptic line). Search for "ASME B106.1M shaft design" and "DE-Goodman shaft criterion".
